tools.title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
tools.summary_raw: FLIPR’s final forecast is in. Here’s why I buy it — mostly.
tools.content_text: Trump with Ken Paxton in Lubbock, Texas on Oct. 27. Paxton is one of the underperforming candidates who could cost Republicans the Senate. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images. FLIPR’s final forecasts are ready for the Senate , House and governorships . Since we’ve recently published some very detailed analysis of basically every race that might matter , I’m not going to go through them state-by-state. Our forecasts show good numbers for Democrats — the last round of polling resolved any doubt about that . They are reasonably clear favorites to flip the Senate, and very likely to flip the House. The Senate is by no means certain, but at the same time, the bottom could fall out for Republicans if Democrats meet or exceed their forecasts on a race-by-race basis. It would be a major surprise if Democrats failed to capture the House, along with various state legislatures and governorships, though some of the most important gubernatorial races like Texas and Florida are “Lean R” rather than the “Lean Ds” that are more typical in the Senate. Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream with The Argument, GD Politics, and Slow Boring. Let’s take roughly three beats here: Returning to where we started when FLIPR launched by considering the background conditions of the election and why they’re so perilous for Republicans — and, I’d argue, ultimately highly consistent with one another. One more quick look at polling error , and why Democrats might be able to survive one in the Senate. And then finally, we’ll try something slightly weirder. I’ll illustrate my “mental map” of the election, and why my gut feels slightly conflicted this time around. But first, a quick word of appreciation. Whether you only come here for election peaks or you're an OG paid subscriber, thank you for following our coverage. Even as compared to 2024, this election has had a really strong finishing kick in the various metrics we track. Subscribe now That’s probably just a reflection of the rhythm of the campaign, though. The most dramatic events of the election two years ago were front-loaded into the summer, and the stretch run was listless, with no presidential debates after Sept. 10. This election has felt more like a typical wave , with Democrats’ advantage building over the course of the cycle . To some extent, this is the usual pattern in midterms. Instead of the back-and-forth that you can get in a presidential year, usually things just get continually worse for one party: Republicans in 2006 and again this year, or Democrats in 2010 and 2014, for instance. Sometimes, like in 1994 and 2014, the actual outcome ends up being even worse than the polls for the party that’s on the back foot. There aren’t many good examples of when the party that seemed to have momentum underperformed — you could sort of argue that for 2022 — though I’m not sure if that’s a durable pattern or something that just reflects small sample sizes. tools.title: How to judge an election model
tools.summary_raw: What would it mean for FLIPR to have a bad night? Plus, more on Haley Stevens and those NYT polls in Still Counting EP9.
tools.content_text: FLIPR is looking pleased with himself, but what if his forecasts turn upside-down? Getty Images. One more newsletter for you before we publish our final FLIPR forecast shortly after midnight. If you’re new here, we do not usually post this much: it’s typically ~3 items a week, not three a day. But we hope you’ll join us for our final flurry of coverage, including our Election Night livestream and live blog tomorrow . Subscribe now And we have a bonus episode of Still Counting out: Reviews, comments, likes and subscribes are always greatly appreciated. Audio version here: The context We covered a lot of ground on the show. But I wrote about those NYT polls and Haley Stevens yesterday, so I’m going to use this as an excuse to cover another topic that Galen, Clare and I were only able to scratch the surface of. I thought it would be nice to write about this ahead of time so it doesn’t feel like spin if a lot of FLIPR’s forecasts don’t come true. I’ll sometimes get the question, “How do you know if a probabilistic forecast is ever really wrong ?” which is an entirely reasonable thing to ask. In fact, let me give you a four-part answer. It’s certainly not quite as simple as saying “30 percent chances are supposed to happen 30 percent of the time.” That’s true insofar as it goes, but it’s incomplete. And if you’re being Bayesian about it, you can’t always use this as a get-of-of-jail-free card. A 0.03 percent chance happening is much more suspect for your model than a 30 percent hitting. First, the canonical way to answer this. You want your probabilistic forecasts to be well-calibrated over a sufficiently large sample of true out-of-sample predictions. In other words, if you’ve forecasted 100 events that you said had a 30 percent probability of happening, and 27 of them or 34 of them actually did “hit”, your model is doing well. The “true out-of-sample predictions” part of the answer is important. Backtesting doesn’t count. Any halfway-competently-designed model should fit the past data well; that’s the easy part. But the model may be misfit or overfit , keying off of essentially random factoids in past data that have no true predictive power and aren’t likely to repeat themselves. You may have noticed that in documenting our models, we tend to not make claims like “ELWAY would have gotten the exact score right in the Super Bowl XVI” or “FLIPR would have nailed the 1994 midterm.” Who cares. We already know what happened. I generally think it’s a negative sign when forecasters brag about their backtested results instead of explaining why they think their models make structural sense. In the case of the Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight lineage of models, however, we have something fairly unique: an 18-year-track record of making true out-of-sample predictions in advance of elections and sporting events, which were published ahead of time, and indeed have received a ton of public scrutiny. tools.title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
tools.summary_raw: Democrats’ Senate odds are boosted by higher-quality candidates. But polls and other data mostly tell a consistent story.
tools.content_text: Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton yesterday in Wichita, Kansas. He’s among the Democrats running more strongly than the “fundamentals”. Jim Vondruska/Getty Images. Political commentators have been obsessed with potential polling error this cycle. And frankly, with the combination of recent high-profile misses and polls looking increasingly like mini-models , it’s hard to blame them. We’ve also covered the topic in some detail , and it can be especially concerning for forecasters when Democrats are putting up their best polling performances in traditionally red states. Some analysts are predicting that the polls will overestimate Democrats as they have in the past few presidential elections: Republican voters can be hard to reach . However, there are also credible arguments for why they could just as easily be underrating Democrats . We think it’s usually a bad idea to try and predict the direction of polling error a priori . But in general, people are hesitant to take the polls at face value this year. In part, that might be because the polls at face value are excellent for Democrats. They lead by 8.9 points in our generic ballot average — that’s a 0.9-point larger lead than they had at this point in 2018. Applying FLIPR’s likely voter adjustment further boosts that lead to D +9.2. Their recent state-level polls are, if anything, even better. We mostly write about our “Deluxe” forecast that incorporates fundamentals and expert ratings, but here’s FLIPR’s “Lite” ( polls only ) Senate forecast. Using the polls alone, FLIPR expects Democrats to easily flip North Carolina, and have about a 75 percent shot in Texas, Ohio, Maine, and (most surprisingly) Kansas. Alaska (63 percent) and Iowa (56 percent) are tougher Democratic flips, while Abdul El-Sayed has an 85 percent chance of holding the Michigan Senate seat — and it’s unlikely the Haley Stevens debacle will change that number. market.title: Theo Bamber, NMA UK: Government Must Act To Protect Trusted Journalism
market.summary_raw: For the annual Journalism Matters campaign, News Media Association Chief Executive Theo Bamber explains why it is more important than ever for governments and regulators to create the right conditions for trusted journalism to thrive.
market.content_text: By Theo Bamber, News Media Association Chief Executive Where does a news story come from? A scandal exposed, a failure revealed, a decision brought into the open that someone would rather have kept private. Behind each is work we rarely see. We read the story, take it in and move on. In short, we take journalism for granted. Someone had to find that story, check it, check it again, and then tell it. That takes skill, experience and painstaking work, sometimes over hours, sometimes over days, weeks, months or years. The published story is the bit we all see, and if we want that to continue, we must protect the people and the industry that makes it possible. This year’s Journalism Matters campaign is a chance for us to reflect carefully on what journalism does for all of us, and what we would lose if we didn’t have it. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda. He is absolutely right to do so. Journalism is part of the national infrastructure we all rely on, and the benefits it delivers go far beyond the stories themselves. A global report published by UNESCO earlier this year found a raft of economic and security benefits connected to journalism in countries with an ecosystem which supports an independent free press. So how do we make sure more journalism can happen? It’s clear that there is plenty the government can do to strengthen the conditions that the industry operates in and it must use this opportunity to affect real change. This should start with digital markets, and creating an ecosystem which can support and maintain a plural and diverse range of media outlets. This increases user choice and allows publishers that invest in reporting to get a fair return for their work. Meta, always ready and willing to play the role of the tech giant bully, recently launched an assault on journalism with its attempt to force publishers and other businesses to hand over all their content to train its AI products. It was a move right out of the tech platform playbook – bury the crucial detail in a ton of paperwork and then feign disbelief and surprise at the horrified reaction from the business community. This can’t continue and, if the government supports journalism in the way the Prime Minister has outlined, it must back the Competition and Markets Authority to the hilt. The CMA is tasked with making the tech platforms play fair, and to do this job effectively it needs full-throated political support. Nothing else will do. But getting the platforms to play fair is just the start. Government must also make sure that its own policies support journalism, not undermine it. The news prominence regime, as proposed in the Media Green Paper, will have a damaging and distortive effect on the news media landscape if implemented in its current form. […]

market.title: Ringier’s ongoing data initiative proves their logged-in users are more valuable – and why
market.summary_raw: The Swiss-based publisher’s Customer Lifetime Value framework is helping them understand why getting people to log in is so important for both reader revenue and advertising.
market.content_text: “For a long time we suspected that logged-in users have a higher value than non-logged-in users, but we didn’t have the data to prove it,” said Patrick Rademacher , Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer, Ringier AG. Founded in 1833, Ringier is a family-owned media and entertainment multi-national group based in Switzerland. The group has three key business areas: media brands, sports media and marketplaces. In total, Ringier owns and operates 115 companies in 19 countries in Europe and Africa with approximately 5,500 employees. About two years ago, Ringier started work on a project to test the hypothesis that logged-in users are more valuable than non-logged-in users, Rademacher said. The efforts focused on Blick , their largest news brand and one of the most popular titles in Switzerland. Bringing the data together A big issue, and one likely to be familiar to many publishers, wasn’t that they actually lacked data, but rather that the data was stored in many different places. “We had data in Google analytics, in the ad server, in the log-in system, etc., etc.,” Rademacher told participants during WAN-IFRA’s recent Digital Media Europe conference in London. “To bring those data together was a lot of work. “ They focused on data around two key areas: Reader revenue and advertising. To determine Customer Lifetime Value, they created a two dimensional approach. The first dimension looks at five different types of users: No consent (meaning website visitors who opt out of sharing their data) Consent only Logged-in users Monthly subscribers Yearly subscribers The second dimension is based on a user’s loyalty, or more specifically, their number of site visits in a given month: One-time readers – those who visit Blick’s site just once in 30 days. Casual readers – two to three visits within 30 days Returning readers – four to 29 visits within 30 days Loyal readers – one to three visits per day Brand lovers – those who visit the site more than three times per day They then combined the two dimensions, creating 25 different user segments, which can be seen in the slide above. A similar approach was taken on the advertising side, Rademacher said. “We have the average revenue per user (ARPU) multiplied by lifetime, which is based on active use, which is partly cookie-based. So this is more complex than reader revenue, but we also got a Customer Lifetime Value, and then brought those two together as one Customer Value,” he said. An ongoing process Rademacher noted that the overall process remains ongoing, and that the findings he was sharing were preliminary. What is important for Ringier now, he said, is the pattern and direction that the early results show. For example, the Customer Lifetime Value of a logged-in user is seven times higher than a user who is not logged-in, he said. They have also found that “t he Customer Lifetime Value of a monthly user is much higher than for a user that has given us only consent,” Rademacher said. […]

market.summary_raw: Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple...
market.content_text: Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI , Google , and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.” Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year. Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping ; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

market.title: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.
market.summary_raw: When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300....
market.content_text: When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.” I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University. Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002. That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it. Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive. Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes , peddle conspiracy theories , rely on low-credibility sources , and sometimes skew to the right . […]
